title: Probing the Person-Patina Relationship: A Correlational Study on the Psychology of Senescent Environments
research_question: To empirically explore the positive and negative psychological perceptions of decay (or patina) on surfaces commonly found in the older built environment, and to identify if these perceptions vary across demographic groups, particularly between historic preservation professionals and laypeople.

participants.description: Adults from the United States, generally younger than the US population, with slightly more males than females. Racial and ethnic demographics were fairly close to the US population. Income tracked fairly close to 2010 US census data. The sample had a higher proportion of antiquarians (33.0%), heritage tourists (60.3%), and individuals working in the historic preservation/CRM field (22.9%) compared to the general US population.
participants.recruitment: Recruited via Amazon's Mechanical Turk (MTurk) service, offering US$1.67 for a 10-minute survey.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 24 images of old, decayed building materials and 7 control images of new building materials. Images were chosen to have a similar distance from target (3-4 feet), flat/direct/head-on perspective, same orientation, similar lighting, and for old materials, a similar level of moderate decay. New materials included brick, stone, wood, concrete, metal, painted, and stucco surfaces.

Likelihood of choosing an 'historic' place to visit for pleasure (dichotomous variable based on Likert scale > 3)
Self-reported employment in public history, historic preservation, or cultural resource management (dichotomous variable)

mechanisms: Ecological Valence Theory (EVT): People like or dislike colors based on the colors of liked or disliked objects in their normal environment, which may explain racial/ethnic differences in material preferences.
Mere Exposure Effect: People tend to like objects that are normally in their environment.
Curved Contours: Materials with smoother, more homogenous, or curved contours are generally preferred over angular ones, which are associated with danger and threats.
Ornamentation and Symmetry: People generally prefer images with symmetrical features and ornamentation, which may explain preferences for certain materials like Stone2 and Copper1.
Biophilia: An innate human affinity for nature, which may explain the positive perception of biological growth like moss (Biogrowth1).

Expertise Divergence: Professionals in historic preservation have a distinct psychological response to decay/patina, valuing it more positively than laypeople, which is termed 'Authorized Heritage Perception' (AHP).
implementation_implications: The findings suggest that the emphasis on retaining patina in historic preservation practice may not align with the general population's values, indicating a potential disconnect between professional doctrine and public perception.
Decision-making processes regarding interventions in the older built environment should consider the differing psychological responses to decay/patina between professionals and laypeople.

limitations: The study only examined visual preferences of surfaces and did not present them within a broader environmental context (e.g., an entire building or landscape), which might influence perceptions.

The study lacked sufficient data to establish whether differences in color preferences between racial/ethnic groups are due to the colors of objects in their normal environments (Ecological Valence Theory).
It is unclear whether the dislike for lichen-covered surfaces (Biogrowth3 and Biogrowth4) is due to the obscuring of the underlying material or a general dislike for lichen itself.
The study could not determine if the preference for Stone3 (new stone) was a rejection of its newness or its contemporary design.
The study did not collect data on whether people living in old/historic neighborhoods exhibit the same increased liking for old, decayed materials as historic preservation professionals.

paper_metadata.title: Probing the Person-Patina Relationship: A Correlational Study on the Psychology of Senescent Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Probing the Person-Patina Relationship: A Correlational Study on the Psychology of Senescent Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: There is a lack of research on people’s psychological perceptions to decay or patina that is part of the historic environment. Built heritage conservation doctrine and law are based on the assumption that all people have a similar, positive aesthetic perception to patina in the built environment, although there are very few empirical studies that have attempted to confirm or challenge this assumption. This study is based on the statistical analysis of survey data from 864 people in the United States who ranked 24 images of old, decayed building materials and 7 control images of new building materials based on aesthetic qualities, condition, and perceived age. The results indicate that people do not like decayed earthen building materials, concrete, or ferrous metals and have a neutral opinion of the aesthetic qualities of aged brick, preferring new brick as well as aged wood. While there are small differences based on race, ethnicity, and gender, the largest difference in responses is between people who work in the historic preservation/CRM field and those who do not. This finding appears to indicate that people who work in these fields have a different psychological response to decay/patina in the built environment than laypeople, which has important ramifications in terms of decision-making processes regarding interventions in the older built environment.

images of new or unaged building materials for comparison

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Aesthetic preferences for environments are significantly influenced by the perceived age and signs of wear (patina) on building materials.
The physical characteristics of an environment, including its signs of age and patina, contribute to the development of emotional bonds and a sense of place.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper likely proposes that the presence of patina on materials influences aesthetic preference through cognitive appraisals of authenticity, history, and character.
